nameStory: The spotted salamander gets its name from the two neat rows of yellow or orange spots that run down its dark back, like bright buttons on a navy coat. These eye-catching spots make it one of the most recognizable salamanders in New England, though some folks also call it the yellow-spotted salamander for the same reason.
description: The spotted salamander is a chunky, robust amphibian that looks like a small, dark sausage decorated with colorful polka dots. Adults typically reach 6-9 inches long and have a sturdy build with relatively short legs and a thick tail. Their dark gray to black skin is marked by two parallel rows of bright yellow, orange, or sometimes reddish spots running from head to tail. This is one of our largest and most commonly encountered salamanders in New England.

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Two distinct rows of bright yellow or orange spots running down a dark gray to black back - these spots are usually round and evenly spaced like decorative buttons

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, moist skin that feels slightly sticky to the touch, with a somewhat slimy coating that helps them breathe through their skin

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Chunky and robust, typically 6-9 inches long with a thick body and relatively short, sturdy legs compared to other salamanders

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found under logs, rocks, or leaf litter in deciduous and mixed forests, especially near seasonal pools or wetlands where they breed

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Small, dark eyes that don't protrude much from the head, giving them a somewhat sleepy appearance

habitat: Spotted salamanders live in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, preferring areas with rich, moist soil and plenty of fallen logs or rocks for cover. They need access to temporary woodland pools or quiet pond edges for breeding, but spend most of their adult lives underground or hidden beneath forest debris. You'll find them in both lowland forests and wooded hillsides up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for spotting them as adults migrate to breeding pools on the first warm, rainy nights of March and April. Look for them crossing roads or gathered in temporary woodland pools where they're laying eggs.
seasonality.summer: Adults retreat underground or deep under logs and rocks to stay cool and moist. Larvae develop in woodland pools, transforming into tiny land-dwelling juveniles by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain mostly hidden underground, though you might find them under logs during mild, wet weather as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: They hibernate underground below the frost line, becoming completely inactive until spring's warm rains trigger their breeding migration.

funFact: Spotted salamander embryos have a secret partnership with green algae that actually live inside their egg capsules, providing oxygen to the developing babies - making them the only known vertebrate with cells that host live-in algae roommates!
confusionNotes: The two neat rows of spots distinguish spotted salamanders from blue-spotted salamanders, which have scattered blue flecks all over their sides and back instead of organized rows. Remember: spotted salamanders wear their spots in orderly lines like military decorations, while blue-spotted salamanders look like they were splattered with blue paint.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mole salamanders,' they don't actually live like moles - the family name refers to their habit of spending most of their time underground or hidden, emerging mainly during breeding season or wet weather.
compareHints: Spotted salamanders are larger and more robust than their blue-spotted cousins, with those distinctive paired rows of spots versus scattered blue markings. They're also much more common than the marbled salamander, which has silvery bands instead of spots and breeds in fall rather than spring. Jefferson salamanders are similar in size but have longer legs and bluish flecks on their sides rather than the neat spotted rows.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue-spotted salamanders are smaller and more slender than spotted salamanders, and their blue markings are unique among New England's mole salamanders.
While spotted salamanders have yellow or orange spots on dark backgrounds, marbled salamanders have white crossbands that go completely across their black bodies.

Among New England's mole salamanders, Jefferson salamanders are the most slender and have the longest toes - much more delicate-looking than the robust Spotted Salamander or the stockier Blue-spotted Salamander.
